phonemes.desc: Voiceless unaspirated bilabial stop [p]; the rough breathing is absent in the Greek spelling.
Close front vowel [y], like French 'tu', with acute stress.
Aspirated voiceless dental stop [tʰ], distinct from English 'th'.
Long open-mid back rounded vowel [ɔː], marked by the macron/circumflex.

pronunciation.approximation: 'PYOO-thohn' — round the lips for 'pyoo', then aspirate the 'th' as in 'top-hon', and hold the final vowel long.

kin.label: Greek
kin.form: Πύθων (Pýthōn), the serpent of Delphi and the name of the place itself.

kin.label: Delphi
kin.form: Pythō, an old name for the sanctuary, from the verb pýthō, 'to rot'.

kin.label: Modern confusion
kin.form: The name was later borrowed for a programming language; the deity has no connection to it.

pronunciation.note: Pýthōn is Tier 1: the Greek original carries both acute stress and a long vowel (ō). The English 'Python' flattens both features.

domains.title: Serpent of Delphi
domains.subtitle: Chthonic Oracle, Slain by Apollo
domains.lead: Pýthōn is the primeval she-serpent who guarded the oracular sanctuary at Delphi. Born from the slime after the flood, she coiled around the omphalos, the navel-stone of the world, until the young Apollo descended from Olympus and slew her. From her corpse the Pythia priestess took her name.

cards.name: Guardian of the Oracle
cards.desc: She protected the chthonic oracle of Gaia at Delphi before Apollo's arrival.

cards.name: Earth Dragon
cards.desc: A child of Gaia, she embodies the earth's primitive, prophetic power.

cards.name: Defeat by Apollo
cards.desc: Apollo's victory over her marks the ascendancy of Olympian prophecy over chthonic earth religion.

cards.name: Pythian Games
cards.desc: The great festival at Delphi commemorated her death with athletic and musical contests.

symbols.name: Serpent/dragon
symbols.meaning: The chthonic power that must be subdued before Apollo can rule Delphi.

symbols.name: Omphalos
symbols.meaning: The navel-stone of the world around which she coiled.

symbols.name: Laurel
symbols.meaning: The plant sacred to Apollo, whose victory over Pýthōn established Delphi's laurel cult.

symbols.name: Tripod
symbols.meaning: The seat of the Pythia priestess who inherited Pýthōn's prophetic voice.

mythology.lead: The myth of Pýthōn is the myth of Apollo's coming-of-age: a young god must kill the ancient serpent to claim his prophetic throne.

myths.title: Birth from the Deluge
myths.text: After Zeus destroyed the earth with a flood, the world was covered in slime. From that decaying mud Gaia produced Pýthōn, a monstrous she-serpent. She made her lair at the foot of Mount Parnassus, where an oracular fissure breathed vapours of prophecy. There she guarded the sanctuary before any Olympian had claimed it.

myths.title: The Slaying of the Serpent
myths.text: Apollo, only four days old in some accounts, travelled to Delphi seeking a place for his oracle. He found Pýthōn coiled around the omphalos and shot her with his arrows. The serpent died, rotting in the sun; the place took the name Pythō from the stench of her corpse (pýthein, 'to rot'). The god then established his temple and his priestess, the Pythia.

myths.title: The Pythia and the Tripod
myths.text: After Pýthōn's death, her prophetic power passed to the Pythia, a woman seated on a tripod above the sacred fissure. Chewing laurel, inhaling vapours, and holding a sprig, she uttered Apollo's responses in hexameter. The serpent was gone, but her name remained in the title of every priestess who followed.

lore.syncretism: Pýthōn belongs to a widespread Indo-European and Near Eastern motif: the young storm or sun god who defeats a primordial dragon to establish cosmic order. The Greek version preserves a specifically Delphic local myth, but echoes of Tiamat, Vṛtra, and the biblical Leviathan are unmistakable. Later Christian writers sometimes identified the Pythian serpent with the devil, though the original Pýthōn was a child of Gaia, not a tempter of humanity.
lore.culturalLegacy: Pýthōn lives on in the Pythian Games, the Pythagorean fascination with Delphi, and the very word 'python'—borrowed, somewhat absurdly, for a programming language whose logo is two snakes. More seriously, the myth remains a foundational text for understanding how Apollo's rational prophecy superseded older, chthonic forms of divination. Every oracle of Delphi, ancient or modern, still stands in the shadow of the serpent he killed.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Pýthōn is the past that must be killed before the future can speak. She is the old oracle, the earth's own voice, the serpent wisdom that predates Olympus. Apollo does not deny her power; he inherits it. The Pythia sits where the serpent coiled; the tripod replaces the coils.

There is something honest in this myth. New institutions rarely arise from empty ground. They come by confronting, incorporating, and renaming what came before. To remember Pýthōn is to remember that every 'new' revelation has an older voice behind it, and that the name of the defeated often outlasts the name of the victor.
lore.originalScriptNote: The Greek is Πύθων, from the verb πύθω ('to rot'), because the serpent's corpse decayed at Delphi. The rough breathing (') on Πύ- indicates an original aspiration; the acute accent marks stress; the final -ων is long. PUNYCODEX writes Pýthōn with the acute and the macron on the long vowel, since the rough breathing is rejected by the DNS root zone.
